title: Death poems
hook: the short verse a Zen teacher leaves at the end of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chan halls in China, rebuilt and filled again, with Pure Land chanting beside the sitting. Your line was the hall is full again. Where did you notice a place coming back to life? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

A brush, an ink stone, and a sheet of paper beside a sickbed. In a Zen temple, an old teacher is near the end, and the students have gathered in the room. Someone grinds the ink. Someone asks, quietly, whether there will be a verse. The teacher takes the brush and writes a few lines, sometimes only a handful of words: the moon, snow on a branch, a breath, even a joke. Then the brush goes down. Zen and Chan tradition kept these short verses, written or spoken at the edge of death, and passed them on with the teaching. Today: death poems.
screen: `A BRUSH BESIDE A SICKBED.` → `A FEW LINES, THEN THE BRUSH GOES DOWN.` → `DEATH POEMS.`

segments.voice: First, the custom. In Japanese a death poem is called jisei, a farewell to the world. Tradition says Chan and Zen teachers were asked for one as the end came near, and their students copied the verses down and kept them. They are short. Some are calm, some are fierce, some are funny. Stories are also told of teachers who refused to write one at all, as if to say the whole life had already been the poem. Second, an older root. Some readers hear an older echo in the Pali suttas. In the sutta on the Buddha's last days, his final words to the monks are short too. In Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Notice what that is. Not a farewell about himself. A last teaching, aimed at the people who would still be alive tomorrow. Third, what a death poem is doing. It isn't a will, and it isn't a list of achievements. Zen teachers spent their lives pointing at this moment: the bowl, the breath, the cypress in the garden. A death poem points at the last moment in the same way. So the subjects are plain things: a cloud, a bird, morning light, empty hands. Death becomes one more thing to see clearly. Fourth, why this belongs on an ordinary day. Writing a few lines about leaving asks a sharp question: what is worth saying last? The answer can be small and ordinary, a window, a name, a cup of tea. The custom doesn't ask for gloom. It asks for attention, while there is still a brush in the hand.
screen: `JISEI: A FAREWELL TO THE WORLD.` · `THE BUDDHA'S LAST WORDS.` · `PLAIN THINGS, SEEN CLEARLY.` · `WHAT IS WORTH SAYING LAST?` · then, large: `A LAST POEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Take a pen, or just use your mind. Make four short lines, with no rules and no rhyme. Line one: something you can see right now. Line two: something you can hear. Line three: one person or one thing you're glad of. Line four: anything at all, or leave it empty. It isn't a goodbye. It's a look around. Then set it down, sit still, and breathe with whatever you made. The bell holds the time.
Death poems. In Japanese, jisei: a short verse left at the end of life in Chan and Zen tradition, usually pointing at something plain and close at hand. Today's word.
Your line: a last poem. Today, when you finish something, a meal, a conversation, a stretch of work, notice its last moment before the next thing begins. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Chan and Zen tradition, teachers near death have traditionally been asked for a short verse, called jisei in Japanese, which students wrote down and kept alongside the teacher's other words.

fork.reveal: death poems are short and point at plain things. a death poem is one more act of seeing clearly, not a will or a résumé.

original.note: Japanese: jisei, a farewell to the world. a death poem is also called jisei no ku (辞世の句).

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad poem about dying.
what it means: a few plain lines at the end, pointing at this moment the way a whole life of practice did.
what a scholar hears: an echo of the Buddha's own last words in the Pali suttas: short, and aimed at the living.
